archetype.name: Playoff Team (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A first-year-coach Bills team that wins with the league's most efficient offense and a strong run game, and needs every point because its defense is the worst in the league by EPA allowed.

report.headline: Elite offense, broken defense: a 6-1 record built for shootouts, not control.
report.take:
Under first-year coach Joe Brady, Buffalo is the league's best offense by EPA per play (0.206) and its best scoring team, with a total of 233 points through seven games. It is also the league's worst defense by the same measure (0.148 EPA allowed, 32nd). Nearly every week has turned into a shootout. The Bills gave up 31, 31, 29, 34 and 30 in five of their first six games and won most of them anyway, because Josh Allen and the run game kept answering. The 36-10 win over Baltimore out of the bye is the only game that looks like the old Bills.

The offense is real, and it is not just Allen. The line ranks 1st in yards before contact (3.27), 2nd in run success and 3rd in stuff rate. It allows pressure on only 18.7% of dropbacks, 5th in the league. James Cook has 138 carries behind that line, and the run game produced 203, 176 and 234 yards in three different wins. Pass EPA ranks 1st at 0.284. This profile has history behind it: Buffalo's offense ranked 2nd to 4th in EPA in each of the last five seasons. What is new is the defense. It ranked 11th or 12th in EPA allowed the last three years and has now fallen to the bottom, 29th against the pass and 27th in missed-tackle rate.

The record runs a little ahead of the play. The point differential implies 4.7 wins, not six (1.29 wins over expected). They have won 80% of one-score games and are minus-2 in turnovers. Netting those out, this is roughly a top-10 team by net EPA (9th), not a juggernaut. The five-turnover win over the Chargers is the clearest case of an offense covering for a mess.

The path ahead favors them. Four of the last nine games are against the Jets and Dolphins, who have one or two wins each. The swing stretch is KC, at New England, at Green Bay, Chicago and at Denver. Whether Buffalo is a contender or just a playoff team comes down to whether Baltimore was a turning point for the defense or a one-off.

strengths.title: League's most efficient offense
strengths.body: Buffalo leads the league in offensive EPA and pass EPA. The offense scores in every kind of game: it posted 41 on Detroit and 37 at the Rams as an underdog. With Allen under center all seven weeks and a five-year track record of top-4 offenses, this is the most bankable part of the team.

strengths.title: A line that wins up front
strengths.body: The run game is efficient, not just a product of game script. The line leads the league in yards before contact and ranks 2nd in run success. It also keeps Allen clean, ranking 5th in pressure rate allowed. That balance lets Buffalo win on the ground when the pass defense is leaking, as in the 234-yard rushing day at the Rams.

strengths.title: Special teams and aggression
strengths.body: Buffalo ranks 4th in special-teams EPA per game and has gone for it on every fourth-down chance the model flags. Both add hidden value in the close games this defense keeps creating.

concerns.title: Pass defense is a sieve
concerns.body: This is a real flaw, not noise. The defense ranks 29th in pass EPA allowed, 30th in success rate allowed and 27th in missed-tackle rate. Opposing WR1s score more over their usual average against Buffalo than against any other defense. It also isn't a sharp drop from a strong baseline: the unit was only middle of the pack the past two seasons, and the Baltimore game is a single data point against six bad ones.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the differential
concerns.body: Six wins against a differential that implies 4.7, an 80% one-score win rate and a negative turnover margin all point to some luck in the record. The offense's ball security is also shaky: it had five turnovers against the Chargers and two in three other games. Close-game luck tends to even out, so expect a couple of these coin flips to go the other way.

concerns.title: Penalties and little pass rush
concerns.body: At 8.3 penalties a game (26th), Buffalo hands drives back, and the defense doesn't get home often enough to erase them (sack rate 25th). The pressure rate (11th) suggests the rush is better than the sack totals. Even so, the penalties look like a discipline issue under a new staff, not a fluke.

trend.note: The offense has scored 24 or more every week. The defense was consistently poor through Week 6, then held Baltimore to 10 points and 91 passing yards coming off the bye, which is one encouraging game rather than a trend yet.

nextGame.headline: Best offense meets best defense in a dome
nextGame.body:
This is a clean strength-on-strength matchup. Minnesota's defense is No. 1 in EPA allowed, pass and run, and leads the league in pressure rate (38.8%) and sack rate. Its offense, though, ranks 30th in EPA, so the Vikings have won by squeezing games: every one-score game has gone their way, they lead the league at +1.2 turnovers a game, and they have 2.52 wins over expected. Buffalo is the better overall team by its offense, and the Book has the Bills -3.5 on the road with a 45.5 total. That total says it expects Minnesota to drag this game to its own pace.

Availability cuts both ways. Buffalo is without OT Spencer Brown, an 88%-snap starter, against the league's best pass rush, plus CB Dee Alford and DT Greg Gaines. DJ Moore (knee) says he's fine, and Joshua Palmer (hamstring) is questionable. For Minnesota, Kyler Murray is questionable with a hamstring and undergoing a full evaluation; Carson Wentz started Week 2 when Murray sat. OT Christian Darrisaw is also questionable, and on a line already allowing the 30th-worst sack rate, that matters.

waysToWin.title: Run at the soft spot
waysToWin.body: Offenses run on Minnesota more than on any other defense relative to the situation. While its rush EPA allowed is strong, it ranks 30th in explosive runs allowed. Buffalo's line, best in the league in yards before contact, can keep Allen out of obvious passing downs and break the chunk runs this defense gives up.

waysToWin.title: Let the Vikings offense stall
waysToWin.body: Minnesota ranks 29th in offensive EPA and 28th in rush EPA, and it allows a sack on 9% of dropbacks. This is the one opponent the Buffalo defense can realistically hold under 20, especially if Murray is limited or Wentz plays. A couple of drive-ending sacks go a long way in a low-total game.

waysToWin.title: Target the WR1, not the tight end
waysToWin.body: Minnesota is the stingiest defense in the league against tight ends, so Kincaid's volume is a poor bet. It is far more generous to opposing WR1s by EPA per target (24th). Feeding Shakir and Moore on early downs is the efficient way to throw on this defense.

waysToLose.title: Pass rush wins on Brown's side
waysToLose.body: With Brown out, Buffalo faces the league's top pressure and sack defense with a backup tackle. If Minnesota can get Buffalo into passing downs, Allen's tendency to force plays plus the offense's minus-2 turnover margin is exactly how the Vikings have won their games.

waysToLose.title: Losing the turnover and field-position game
waysToLose.body: Minnesota leads the league in turnover differential and special-teams EPA, and allows red-zone touchdowns only 23% of the time. A short field or a red-zone stall can flip a game Buffalo controls between the 20s, the way New England did in Week 4.

waysToLose.title: The defense rescues a bad offense
waysToLose.body: Even a 30th-ranked offense can move the ball on a unit that ranks last in EPA allowed and 27th in missed tackles. Without Alford in the secondary, Buffalo can give up the explosive pass that a low-scoring game can't absorb.

nextGame.watch: Buffalo's early-down run success against Minnesota's run-funnel defense. If Cook stays on schedule, Brown's absence never gets exposed to that pass rush.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should stay at or near the top of the league. It has a proven quarterback, a line that wins in both phases and a five-year track record of elite offenses. Some scoring regression from its current pace is normal, but this is a 27-to-32-point team, not a fluke. The defense is where the range sits. Its last three seasons sat in the middle of the league, and the Baltimore game showed what it looks like when it tackles and gets home, so modest improvement from last place is plausible. A return to a good defense is not something to count on.

The record will probably regress toward the efficiency in close games. The schedule cushions that: four games against Miami and New York should bank wins, and the KC-to-Denver stretch decides seeding. Expect a division winner in the 11-to-13-win range that wins most games by outscoring opponents.
swingFactors: Whether the Baltimore defensive performance carries over
Spencer Brown's return and line health

confidence.note: Seven games is a small sample. The offense has strong history behind it, but the defense's collapse is new.
